misaligned_misconception.name: Carry-Not-Reset
misaligned_misconception.description: A systematic procedural bug in addition where the student forgets to reset the carry register to zero after processing each column. Instead of resetting the carry after adding it to a column, the carry value accumulates across columns. For example, in 328 + 917, the student writes 5 (from 8+7=15), carries 1, then computes 2+1+1=4, but instead of resetting the carry to 0, keeps it at 1. In the next column, 3+9+1=13, so the final answer is 1345 instead of 1245. This bug was identified by Brown & Burton (1978) in their BUGGY diagnostic system for arithmetic procedures.

misconception: Student forgets to raise coefficient to the outer power: (cx^m)^n = c·x^(mn). For example, (2x³)⁵ = 2x¹⁵ instead of 32x¹⁵. Research identifies this as part of the broader 'failure to consider parentheses when performing operations' (Egodawatte, 2011).

misaligned_misconception.name: Mean-Without-Understanding
misaligned_misconception.description: Students calculate mean procedurally (add all values, divide by count) without understanding what it represents. Research shows many students know how to compute means but do not know how to apply or interpret them (Konold & Pollatsek, 2002). They correctly compute the mean but: (1) claim it's always representative even with outliers, (2) always say mean is the 'best' measure regardless of distribution, (3) don't recognize when mean is misleading, and (4) can't explain what the mean tells them about the data.

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where the student aligns numbers on the left side instead of the right side (place value alignment) when adding numbers of different digit lengths. This causes the shorter number to be effectively multiplied by a power of 10. For example, in 23 + 456, the student aligns 23 with the left side of 456, treating 23 as 230, yielding 686 instead of the correct answer 479. This is documented in Brown & Burton's 1978 paper on diagnostic models for procedural bugs in basic mathematical skills.

misaligned_misconception.description: A systematic procedural bug where the student stops the borrowing (regrouping) process entirely when encountering a zero in the column to the left, rather than cascading the borrow further left to find a non-zero digit. This bug is part of a family of zero-related borrowing errors documented in VanLehn's 'Mind Bugs' (1990) and the BUGGY/DEBUGGY diagnostic systems. When students reach an impasse at zero, they may write the absolute difference or simply give up on that column.

misconception: Students incorrectly compare fractions by comparing their numerators only, ignoring the denominators entirely. They believe that a larger numerator means a larger fraction. For example: 3/4 < 5/8 because 3 < 5 (incorrect). misaligned_misconception.name: No-Column-Limit
misaligned_misconception.description: When adding multi-digit numbers, students write the entire column sum directly in that column without regrouping, failing to understand the base-10 constraint that each place value position can only hold a single digit (0-9). For example, in 48+17, students compute 8+7=15 and write '15' in the ones column, producing concatenated results like '415' instead of the correct answer 65. This error, documented by the Colorado Department of Education, indicates a fundamental misunderstanding of place value.

This is documented as one of the most common errors in dimensional analysis, where students fail to ensure that units cancel appropriately.

misaligned_misconception.name: Incomplete-Factoring
misaligned_misconception.description: Students terminate the factoring process prematurely, stopping after one factoring step without recognizing that further factorization is possible. For example, writing 2x² - 8 = 2(x² - 4) instead of the complete factorization 2(x+2)(x-2). This reflects a procedural rather than conceptual understanding of what 'factor completely' means (Kieran, 1992; Vaiyavutjamai & Clements, 2006).

misconception: Students confuse the solution patterns for absolute value inequalities, applying the 'less than' pattern (three-part inequality) to 'greater than' problems and vice versa. Research shows this error affects 12-27% of students on specific problem types, stemming from failure to connect the inequality direction to geometric meaning (inside vs. outside an interval on the number line).

This is: 'x is between -20 and 20, inclusive'
This is a three-part inequality with x in the closed interval [-20, 20]. We can verify: x=20 should work, and |20| = 20 ≤ 20 ✓

misaligned_misconception.name: Forget-Borrow-Over-Blanks
misaligned_misconception.description: A systematic procedural bug where the student forgets to borrow over blank columns when the minuend (top number) has fewer digits than the subtrahend (bottom number). The student incorrectly processes the 'blank' positions (implicit zeros) without properly propagating borrows. For example, in 85 - 127, the student may treat the hundreds column as simply 1-0 or 0-1 (using smaller-from-larger), yielding an incorrect positive result instead of recognizing that the operation produces a negative number or requires special handling. This bug is located in the COLUMN SEQUENCE procedure of Brown & Burton's procedural network.

misconception: Students use the 'transition model' of algebraic manipulation, incorrectly believing that moving a term across the equals sign simply requires changing its sign. They do not understand that solving equations requires applying inverse operations to both sides to maintain equality. This reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of the equals sign as a relational symbol.

This bug occurs in the COMPLETE COLUMN procedure when students see a 0 in the minuend and simply write 0 without considering that borrowing is required. This is documented in Brown & Burton's (1978) BUGGY system. Example: 140 - 21 = 120 (correct: 119)

misconception: Students incorrectly apply the multiplication rule 'two negatives make a positive' to subtraction and addition operations. This represents what Makonye & Fakude (2016) term 'surface understanding' where students remember rules like 'negative and negative becomes positive' and apply them indiscriminately across operations. For example, students compute -5 - 6 = 11 because they see the negative sign in -5 and the subtraction operation as 'two negatives' that should combine to make a positive result. Vlassis (2004) identifies this as stemming from students' failure to distinguish between the 'operative sign' (subtraction) and the 'unary, predicative sign' (negativity of a number).

misaligned_misconception.name: Add-All-Digits
misaligned_misconception.description: A systematic procedural bug where the student always sums up all the digits with no regard to columns or place value. For example, in 17 + 5, the student computes 1 + 7 + 5 = 13 instead of correctly aligning and adding to get 22. This is documented in Brown & Burton (1978) as one of the fundamental addition bugs that shows complete misunderstanding of place value.

misconception:
A compound procedural bug where the student's multiplication algorithm mimics the column behavior of addition---multiplying column by column instead of digit by digit. The student processes corresponding digits in each column (like in addition), but multiplies them instead of adding. Additionally, the student applies the WRITE/CARRY/FORGET/UNITS bug: when a column product is 10 or greater, they write only the carry digit (tens place) and forget the units digit. For products less than 10, they write the result normally.

Example: 68 x 46 = 24 (correct: 3128)

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where students correctly compute partial products but fail to align them properly according to place value. misconception: Students confuse -√n with √-n, failing to recognize that the domain of the radical function is restricted to nonnegative real numbers. They incorrectly believe that -√4 has no real solution because they treat the negative sign outside the radical as if it were inside. Research shows students are 'not aware that the domain of radical function is nonnegative real numbers' (Özkan, 2011), leading them to misinterpret valid expressions as undefined.

This would be the square root of a negative number
The student confused the placement of the negative sign. The negative is OUTSIDE the radical, not inside it.

misconception: Student incorrectly applies the multiplicative (homogeneous) property of linear functions to nonlinear functions: f(cx) = c·f(x). This is a manifestation of the 'illusion of linearity' (De Bock et al., 2007), where students overgeneralize properties that hold only for linear functions f(x) = kx. Matz (1982) identified f(ka) = kf(a) as a common algebraic error.

problems.problem_text: Given f(x) = |x + 2|, evaluate f(4×2)
correct_steps: CORRECT METHOD: Substitute the entire expression
f(4×2) means substitute '4×2' for 'x' in f(x) = |x + 2|
Remember: f(cx) ≠ c·f(x) for most functions!
malrule_steps: MALRULE: Factor out the scalar (treating input and output multiplication as the same)
f(4×2) = 4 · f(2)  [WRONG! Can't factor out scalar from input]
WRONG! With f(x) = |x + 2|, we have f(4×2) = |4×2 + 2| = 10, NOT 4·|2 + 2| = 16. The student confuses input and output multiplication.
The fundamental error: Confusing f(cx) with c·f(x). Input multiplication and output multiplication are NOT the same!

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where the student writes the carry digit and forgets to write the units digit in the answer when a column sum is 10 or more. For example, in 87 + 93, the student computes 7+3=10, writes 1 (the carry digit) instead of 0, then 8+9=17, writes 1 (the carry digit) instead of 7, yielding 11 instead of the correct answer 180. This bug was documented by Brown & Burton (1978) in their analysis of systematic procedural errors in arithmetic.

When multiplying by decimals or fractions less than 1 (e.g., 0.5 × 0.2 = 0.1), students reject the correct answer as impossible because the product is smaller than both factors. They may substitute addition or refuse to accept the mathematically correct result.

Example: 304 - 75 = 139 (correct: 229)
The student skips the 0 when borrowing for ones column, then has to borrow again when processing the tens column (0-7).

misconception: Student multiplies exponents when multiplying powers with the same base: x^m × x^n = x^(m×n). For example, x³ × x⁵ = x¹⁵ instead of x⁸. Research documents this as confusion between the product rule (add) and power rule (multiply).

correct_steps: When multiplying powers with the same base, ADD the exponents:
x^3 × x^2 × x^3 = x multiplied by itself (3+2+3) = 8 times
The product rule states that when multiplying powers with the same base, we add the exponents.
malrule_steps: The student incorrectly multiplies the exponents. This confuses the product rule (add exponents) with the power rule (multiply exponents for (x^m)^n).

misconception: Students incorrectly keep the common denominator when multiplying fractions with like denominators: (a/b)×(c/b) = (a×c)/b instead of (a×c)/(b×b). For example, (2/5)×(3/5) = 6/5 instead of the correct answer 6/25. This is an overgeneralization error where students apply the fraction addition rule (keep the common denominator) to multiplication. Newton et al. (2014) found students were particularly prone to this error on like-denominator problems.

correct_steps: Problem: A garden bed is 3/5 of an acre. The vegetable section is 3/5 of that, and the herb section is 3/5 of the vegetable section. What fraction of an acre is the herb section?
CORRECT METHOD: Multiply numerators AND denominators
To multiply fractions, we multiply numerators AND denominators. Even though fractions share denominator 5, we still multiply it.
malrule_steps: Problem: A garden bed is 3/5 of an acre. The vegetable section is 3/5 of that, and the herb section is 3/5 of the vegetable section. What fraction of an acre is the herb section?
MALRULE: Keep the common denominator (treating multiplication like addition)
Both fractions have denominator 5, so keep it
The student incorrectly keeps the common denominator 5, overgeneralizing the addition rule to multiplication. In multiplication, we must multiply both numerators AND denominators.

misconception:
A compound procedural bug where the student's multiplication algorithm mimics the column behavior of addition---multiplying column by column instead of digit by digit. The student processes corresponding digits in each column (like in addition), but multiplies them instead of adding. Additionally, the student applies the WRITE/CARRY/FORGET/UNITS bug: when a column product is 10 or greater, they write only the carry digit (tens place) and forget the units digit. For products less than 10, they write the result normally.

Example: 68 x 46 = 24 (correct: 3128)
  - Column 1 (ones): 8 x 6 = 48, writes 4 (the carry), forgets 8
  - Column 2 (tens): 6 x 4 = 24, writes 2 (the carry), forgets 4
  - Final answer: 24

misconception: Students calculate mean procedurally (add all values, divide by count) without understanding what it represents. Research shows many students know how to compute means but do not know how to apply or interpret them (Konold & Pollatsek, 2002). They correctly compute the mean but: (1) claim it's always representative even with outliers, (2) always say mean is the 'best' measure regardless of distribution, (3) don't recognize when mean is misleading, and (4) can't explain what the mean tells them about the data.

misconception: Students don't recognize how outliers affect the mean. Research shows students are 'not only confused about the median and the mean but also unable to use and interpret information' about when each is appropriate (Zawojewski & Shaughnessy, 2000). misconception: A systematic procedural bug in addition where the student forgets to reset the carry register to zero after processing each column. misconception: Student forgets to raise coefficient to the outer power: (cx^m)^n = c·x^(mn). For example, (2x³)⁵ = 2x¹⁵ instead of 32x¹⁵. Research identifies this as part of the broader 'failure to consider parentheses when performing operations' (Egodawatte, 2011).

problems.problem_text: A gravitational field strength is (3x^3y^3)^3. Simplify this expression.
correct_steps: Word Problem: A gravitational field strength is (3x^3y^3)^3. Simplify this expression.
Step 1: Extract the mathematical expression from the word problem
Step 2: Apply the power of a power rule - raise EVERYTHING to outer power
Step 3: Raise coefficient to outer power
Step 4: Multiply exponents for each variable
The key is that the outer exponent applies to EVERYTHING inside the parentheses. We must raise both the coefficient and apply the power rule to variables.
malrule_steps: Word Problem: A gravitational field strength is (3x^3y^3)^3. Simplify this expression.
Step 1: Extract the mathematical expression from the word problem
Step 2: Apply malrule (incorrectly forget to raise coefficient)
MALRULE: Apply power rule to variables only, forget coefficient
Step 3: Multiply exponents for each variable

The student correctly multiplied the exponents for the variables but forgot to raise the coefficient to the outer power. They don't understand that the outer exponent applies to EVERYTHING inside the parentheses, including the coefficient.

Step 1: Multiply the exponents for the variable

The student correctly multiplied the exponents for the variables but forgot to raise the coefficient to the outer power. They don't understand that the outer exponent applies to EVERYTHING inside the parentheses, including the coefficient.

misconception: Student incorrectly applies the additive property of linear functions to nonlinear functions: f(x+a) = f(x) + f(a). This error, termed the 'illusion of linearity' by De Bock et al. (2007), results from overgeneralization of the distributive law experienced extensively in arithmetic and early algebra (Matz, 1982).

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where the student always subtracts the smaller digit from the larger digit in each column, regardless of position (minuend or subtrahend). This error avoids borrowing by reversing the subtraction when the top digit is smaller than the bottom digit. For example, in 62 - 37, the student computes 7-2=5 in the ones column (instead of borrowing) and 6-3=3 in the tens column, yielding 35 instead of the correct answer 25. This is one of the most extensively documented subtraction bugs in cognitive science research, identified through the BUGGY and DEBUGGY diagnostic systems.

misconception: A widespread misconception where students believe multiplication always produces a result larger than both factors. Fischbein et al. (1985) identified this as stemming from the 'primitive intuitive model' of multiplication as repeated addition, where results are always larger with whole numbers. When multiplying by decimals or fractions less than 1 (e.g., 0.5 × 0.2 = 0.1), students reject the correct answer as impossible because the product is smaller than both factors. They may substitute addition or refuse to accept the mathematically correct result.

problems.problem_text: A rectangular garden is 0.9 meters long and 0.8 meters wide. What is its area in square meters?
correct_steps: Problem: A rectangular garden is 0.9 meters long and 0.8 meters wide. What is its area in square meters?
CORRECT METHOD: Understanding multiplication with numbers < 1
KEY INSIGHT: Both factors are less than 1
Either way, we're taking a fraction of a fraction, which is smaller
CORRECT - multiplying by a number < 1 makes it smaller!
malrule_steps: Problem: A rectangular garden is 0.9 meters long and 0.8 meters wide. What is its area in square meters?
MALRULE: Multiplication always makes numbers bigger
But 0.7200 is smaller than 0.9! This can't be right...
MALRULE REASONING: Multiplication must make it bigger!
Answer: 1.7000 meters (INCORRECT - added instead of multiplied)
Error: Student doesn't understand multiplication by numbers < 1

problems.problem_text: A coin has a 0.4 chance of landing heads. If you flip it twice, and the probability of a certain outcome on the second flip is 0.6, what is the probability of both outcomes occurring?
correct_steps: Problem: A coin has a 0.4 chance of landing heads. If you flip it twice, and the probability of a certain outcome on the second flip is 0.6, what is the probability of both outcomes occurring?
CORRECT METHOD: Understanding multiplication with numbers < 1
Compound probability: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)
KEY INSIGHT: Both factors are less than 1
Either way, we're taking a fraction of a fraction, which is smaller
CORRECT - multiplying by a number < 1 makes it smaller!
malrule_steps: Problem: A coin has a 0.4 chance of landing heads. If you flip it twice, and the probability of a certain outcome on the second flip is 0.6, what is the probability of both outcomes occurring?
MALRULE: Multiplication always makes numbers bigger
But 0.2400 is smaller than 0.6! This can't be right...
MALRULE REASONING: Multiplication must make it bigger!
Error: Student doesn't understand multiplication by numbers < 1

misconception: A widespread misconception where students believe division always produces a result smaller than the dividend. Fischbein et al. (1985) identified this as a 'primitive intuitive model' stemming from early division experiences with whole numbers. When dividing by decimals or fractions less than 1 (which mathematically produces a larger result), students reject the correct answer as impossible and switch to multiplication. For example, students find 4 ÷ 0.5 = 8 counterintuitive and switch to 4 × 0.5 = 2 instead.

misconception: Students treat percent, decimal, and whole number notations as interchangeable, failing to recognize that percent means 'per hundred' and requires division by 100 to convert to decimal form. This reflects a broader difficulty with rational number notation where students do not understand that different symbolic representations indicate the same underlying quantity through different numerical expressions.

misconception: Students incorrectly believe that decimals with fewer decimal places are larger. For example, they think 0.3 is larger than 0.496. This misconception is linked to denominator-focused thinking, reciprocal thinking, or fraction knowledge interference (Steinle & Stacey, 1998; Resnick et al., 1989).

misconception: Student swaps the roles of slope (m) and y-intercept (b) in y = mx + b, either writing equations with parameters reversed or identifying the constant term as slope and the coefficient as y-intercept. This reflects confusion about the distinct structural roles of coefficient and constant in function notation.

misconception: Students confuse -√n with √-n, failing to recognize that the domain of the radical function is restricted to nonnegative real numbers. They incorrectly believe that -√4 has no real solution because they treat the negative sign outside the radical as if it were inside. Research shows students are 'not aware that the domain of radical function is nonnegative real numbers' (Özkan, 2011), leading them to misinterpret valid expressions as undefined.

correct_steps: Problem: An object has velocity -√36 m/s. If this velocity is scaled by a factor of 3, what is the new velocity? (Calculate: 3(-√36))
CORRECT METHOD: The negative sign is OUTSIDE the radical
Key: The negative OUTSIDE the radical means 'opposite of the square root', which is valid. Different from √-n which is undefined in reals.

This would be the square root of a negative number
The student confused the placement of the negative sign. The negative is OUTSIDE the radical, not inside it.

misconception: Students incorrectly apply additive reasoning to percentage problems that require multiplicative thinking. They add or subtract percentages directly without recognizing that each percentage applies to a different base value. This reflects a fundamental gap in the transition from additive to multiplicative reasoning, which is one of the major barriers to mathematical development (Van Dooren, De Bock, & Verschaffel, 2010).

misconception: Students incorrectly believe that multiplication must ALWAYS be performed before division. They interpret PEMDAS literally on a letter-by-letter basis, following the order of 'M' and 'D' to incorrectly believe that multiplication must be performed before division (Eaves et al., 2025). Example: 6 ÷ 2 × 3 becomes 6 ÷ 6 = 1 instead of 9.

A systematic procedural bug where when borrowing into a column whose ORIGINAL top digit is 1, the student gets 10 instead of 11. The student treats the borrowed 10 as replacing the existing digit rather than adding to it. This bug occurs in the ADD TEN procedure of the subtraction algorithm and only applies to digits that were originally 1 in the problem.

Example: 321 - 89 = 231 (correct: 232)

- When borrowing into this column, 1 + 10 should = 11
- Student incorrectly gets 10 (ignoring the existing 1)
- 10 - 9 = 1 instead of 11 - 9 = 2

This stems from overgeneralizing whole number comparison rules to decimals, a phenomenon extensively documented by Steinle & Stacey (1998, 2004) as one of the most prevalent decimal misconceptions.

This overgeneralization leads to errors like (a+b)² = a² + b² (missing the middle term) and √(a+b) = √a + √b (incorrectly distributing the square root).

misconception: Students make sign errors when factoring quadratics, selecting incorrect signs for the binomial factors. This is classified as a procedural error involving mishandling of signs (Tendere & Mutambara, 2020). Research indicates this is one of the most common errors in quadratic equation solving, with students finding the correct factor magnitudes but applying incorrect sign patterns.

This is documented as one of the most common errors in dimensional analysis, where students fail to ensure that units cancel appropriately.

This error reflects 'whole number bias' (Ni & Zhou, 2005) - the overgeneralization of whole-number comparison rules where larger numbers always mean 'more.' Students fail to understand the inverse relationship: larger denominators mean smaller pieces.

misconception: Students incorrectly distribute absolute value over addition or subtraction, treating |a+b| as |a|+|b|. This is an overgeneralization of the distributive property, where students apply learned algebraic rules (like distribution) to functions where they do not apply. The absolute value bars are visually similar to parentheses, reinforcing this erroneous application.

The student incorrectly distributes the absolute value. They treat |x + 10| as if absolute value distributes over operations, but it does NOT. The correct approach is to evaluate x + 10 first, then take the absolute value of the result.

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where the student aligns numbers on the left side instead of the right side (place value alignment) when adding numbers of different digit lengths. This causes the shorter number to be effectively multiplied by a power of 10. For example, in 23 + 456, the student aligns 23 with the left side of 456, treating 23 as 230, yielding 686 instead of the correct answer 479. This is documented in Brown & Burton's 1978 paper on diagnostic models for procedural bugs in basic mathematical skills.

misconception: Students confuse the solution patterns for absolute value inequalities, applying the 'less than' pattern (three-part inequality) to 'greater than' problems and vice versa. Research shows this error affects 12-27% of students on specific problem types, stemming from failure to connect the inequality direction to geometric meaning (inside vs. outside an interval on the number line).

malrule_steps: MALRULE: Student applies 'greater than' pattern to 'less than' inequality

The student incorrectly applies the greater-than pattern (two separate regions) to a less-than inequality. They don't understand that |x| < 8 means x is WITHIN 8 units of 0, not outside.

misconception: Students don't recognize how outliers affect the mean. Research shows students are 'not only confused about the median and the mean but also unable to use and interpret information' about when each is appropriate (Zawojewski & Shaughnessy, 2000). When asked if the mean represents a data set with outliers, they say 'yes' without understanding that outliers pull the mean away from typical values. They fail to identify that median is more appropriate for skewed data.

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where students correctly compute partial products but fail to align them properly according to place value. When multiplying by the tens digit, students do not shift the partial product one place to the left, treating the tens digit as if it were in the ones place. For example, in 23 × 14, they compute 23×4=92 and 23×1=23, then add 92+23=115 instead of 92+230=322. This error was documented in Brown & Burton's (1978) BUGGY diagnostic system as a common procedural bug in multi-digit arithmetic algorithms.

problems.problem_text: On a map, 114 centimeters represents 34 kilometers. Write the simplified ratio of map distance to actual distance.
correct_steps: Problem: On a map, 114 centimeters represents 34 kilometers. Write the simplified ratio o...
CORRECT METHOD: Find GCD and divide both terms
Step 1: Find the GCD of 114 and 34
Method: Prime factorization or Euclidean algorithm
Step 2: Divide both terms by the GCD
malrule_steps: Problem: On a map, 114 centimeters represents 34 kilometers. Write the simplified ratio o...
MALRULE: Treat each digit as a separate ratio
MALRULE REASONING: 'Each digit pair is its own fraction'
Step 2: Simplify each digit pair independently
WHY WRONG: 114 is not '1 and 1', it's 114!

When the leftmost digits form '10', the student recognizes this as a special case and borrows correctly. Otherwise, they apply the standard borrow-from-zero bug, writing 9 in place of 0 without decrementing the next column.

misconception: Students terminate the factoring process prematurely, stopping after one factoring step without recognizing that further factorization is possible. For example, writing 2x² - 8 = 2(x² - 4) instead of the complete factorization 2(x+2)(x-2). This reflects a procedural rather than conceptual understanding of what 'factor completely' means (Kieran, 1992; Vaiyavutjamai & Clements, 2006).

problems.problem_text: The expression 4x² + 16x + 16 represents the total area of a tiled floor. Factor completely.
correct_steps: Word Problem: The expression 4x² + 16x + 16 represents the total area of a tiled floor. Factor completely.
Step 1: Extract the expression from the word problem
Strategy: Factor until no more factoring is possible
Step 4: Recognize the perfect square trinomial
Check: Is this a perfect square?
Final Step: Verify it's completely factored
Each factor is either a number or linear (cannot factor further)
malrule_steps: Word Problem: The expression 4x² + 16x + 16 represents the total area of a tiled floor. Factor completely.
Step 1: Extract the expression from the word problem
Step 2: Factor (but student stops too early)
MALRULE: Stop after first factoring step (incomplete)
Student thinks: 'I factored out the GCF, I'm done!'
WRONG! The trinomial x² + 4x + 4 is a perfect square! Notice: 4 = 2 × 2 and 4 = 2². So x² + 4x + 4 = (x + 2)². The complete factorization is 4(x + 2)².
The fundamental error: Stopping before complete factorization!

problems.problem_text: The total area of 2 identical rectangular plots is 2x² + 10x + 8 square meters. Factor completely to find the dimensions of each plot.
correct_steps: Word Problem: The total area of 2 identical rectangular plots is 2x² + 10x + 8 square meters. Factor completely to find the dimensions of each plot.
Step 1: Extract the expression from the word problem
Strategy: Factor until no more factoring is possible
Need two numbers that multiply to 4 and add to 5
Final Step: Verify it's completely factored
Each factor is either a number or linear (cannot factor further)
malrule_steps: Word Problem: The total area of 2 identical rectangular plots is 2x² + 10x + 8 square meters. Factor completely to find the dimensions of each plot.
Step 1: Extract the expression from the word problem
Step 2: Factor (but student stops too early)
MALRULE: Stop after first factoring step (incomplete)
Student thinks: 'I factored out the GCF, I'm done!'
WRONG! The trinomial x² + 5x + 4 can be factored further! It factors as (x + 4)(x + 1) since 4 × 1 = 4 and 4 + 1 = 5. The complete factorization is 2(x + 4)(x + 1).
The fundamental error: Stopping before complete factorization!

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where, when a column sum exceeds 9, the student adds the units digit and carry digit together and writes that combined result in the current column. The carry is NOT propagated to the next column. For example, in 17 + 5, the ones column computes 7+5=12, then the student adds 1+2=3 and writes 3 in the ones column. The tens column then computes 1+0=1. Result: 13 instead of 22. This bug may arise from confusion about Method 2 (left-to-right addition) where carries are written under the same column.

Write 0 in tens place, carry 1 to hundreds place
malrule_steps: When column sum > 9, add units digit and carry digit together
Tens place: 4 + 6 = 10 (more than 9), so add units and carry: 0 + 1 = 1, write 1

Write 6 in ones place, carry 1 to tens place
malrule_steps: When column sum > 9, add units digit and carry digit together
Ones place: 7 + 9 = 16 (more than 9), so add units and carry: 6 + 1 = 7, write 7

misconception: Students calculate mean procedurally (add all values, divide by count) without understanding what it represents. Research shows many students know how to compute means but do not know how to apply or interpret them (Konold & Pollatsek, 2002). They correctly compute the mean but: (1) claim it's always representative even with outliers, (2) always say mean is the 'best' measure regardless of distribution, (3) don't recognize when mean is misleading, and (4) can't explain what the mean tells them about the data.

problems.malrule_answer: Yes, the mean of 97.45 is representative of the typical value.

This suggests data is skewed or has outliers

Final answer: No, the mean (97.45) is NOT representative. The median (55.00) better represents the typical value because outliers skew the mean.

Calculating mean: sum of all values ÷ count
MALRULE THINKING: Mean is always representative
MALRULE ANSWER: Yes, the mean of 97.45 is representative of the typical value.
MALRULE ERROR: Doesn't recognize outliers make mean non-representative!

misconception: When subtracting fractions with different denominators, students incorrectly subtract the numerators AND subtract the denominators: a/b - c/d = (a-c)/(b-d). For example: 3/4 - 1/2 = (3-1)/(4-2) = 2/2 = 1 (incorrect; correct answer is 1/4). Brown & Quinn (2006) documented this error in their analysis of algebra students' fraction errors, finding that students 'demonstrated the error of adding or subtracting numerators and denominators across' by extending whole number operations to fractions.

This is one of the most common and persistent misconceptions in algebra, documented across multiple levels and educational contexts.

This is documented as one of the most common errors in dimensional analysis, where students fail to ensure that units cancel appropriately.

misconception: Students use the 'transition model' of algebraic manipulation, incorrectly believing that moving a term across the equals sign simply requires changing its sign. They do not understand that solving equations requires applying inverse operations to both sides to maintain equality. This reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of the equals sign as a relational symbol.

misconception: Students incorrectly compare fractions by comparing their numerators only, ignoring the denominators entirely. They believe that a larger numerator means a larger fraction. For example: 3/4 < 5/8 because 3 < 5 (incorrect). This is a manifestation of the 'natural number bias' or 'whole number bias'—the tendency to apply natural number properties inappropriately to rational numbers.

Step 2: Convert each fraction to equivalent fraction with common denominator

misconception: Students incorrectly believe that percentage relationships are symmetric or reversible. They assume that if a value increased by X%, it can return to the original by decreasing X%, or that if A is X% of B, then B is X% of A. This misconception stems from overgeneralizing the commutative property of addition and multiplication to percentage relationships, which are inherently asymmetric because each percentage is calculated relative to a different base value.

problems.problem_text: A stock price rose from $89 to $107 (20% gain). If it falls back to $89, what is the percent loss?
correct_steps: Problem: A stock price rose from $89 to $107 (20% gain). If it falls back to $89, what is the percent loss?
Step 2: Calculate percent decrease (base = NEW value)
Key insight: Percentage relationships depend on the BASE value!
malrule_steps: Problem: A stock price rose from $89 to $107 (20% gain). If it falls back to $89, what is the percent loss?
MALRULE REASONING: 'The percentage is the same going both directions'
INCORRECT! Percentage relationships are NOT symmetric.
The percentage depends on which value is the base (denominator).

problems.problem_text: A value decreased from 277 to 166, which is a 40% decrease. If the value increases from 166 back to 277, what is the percent increase?
correct_steps: Problem: Value decreased from 277 to 166 (40% decrease).
What is the percent increase from 166 back to 277?
Step 2: Calculate percent increase (use NEW value as base)
Note: 40% decrease requires 66.9% increase to reverse
The percentages are NOT the same!
Key insight: Percentage relationships depend on the BASE value!
malrule_steps: Problem: Value decreased from 277 to 166 (40% decrease).
What is the percent increase from 166 back to 277?
MALRULE: Decrease and increase percentages are symmetric
MALRULE REASONING: 'If it decreased by 40%, it must increase by 40%'
INCORRECT! Percentage relationships are NOT symmetric.
The percentage depends on which value is the base (denominator).

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where the student aligns numbers on the left side instead of the right side (place value alignment) when adding numbers of different digit lengths. This causes the shorter number to be effectively multiplied by a power of 10. For example, in 23 + 456, the student aligns 23 with the left side of 456, treating 23 as 230, yielding 686 instead of the correct answer 479. This is documented in Brown & Burton's 1978 paper on diagnostic models for procedural bugs in basic mathematical skills.

correct_steps: CORRECT METHOD: Right-align by place value
Align from the right (ones place with ones place)
malrule_steps: Problem: A box contains 9430 books and another box contains 58971 books. What is the total number of books?
Student belief: 'Numbers should be aligned from the left'
9430 is treated as 94300 (padded with 1 zero(s) on right)

problems.problem_text: What is 158 + 16?
correct_steps: CORRECT METHOD: Right-align by place value
Align from the right (ones place with ones place)
malrule_steps: Student belief: 'Numbers should be aligned from the left'

misconception: Students incorrectly determine the sign of the result by always using the sign of the number with the larger absolute value, regardless of the operation. This represents an overgeneralization from addition of integers with different signs (where the rule works) to all integer operations. Makonye & Fakude (2016) classify this as a 'strategic error' where students apply a partially-correct strategy inappropriately. For subtraction like 3 - (-8), students incorrectly reason: '|8| > |3|, so use -8's sign' → -11 (wrong! correct answer is +11).

problems.problem_text: Calculate: (18) ÷ (-6)

Final Answer: 3 (INCORRECT - sign rule doesn't depend only on magnitude!)

misconception: When interpreting place value decompositions, the student treats the numeric labels as face values to be concatenated rather than as multiplicative values to be added. For example, '2 hundreds 13 tens 1 ones' is written as 2,131 instead of correctly calculating 200 + 130 + 1 = 331. This error reflects what Ross (1989) identified as 'face value' understanding - students interpret digits at their literal face value without understanding their positional significance. The student perceives the decomposition as a labeling task rather than a mathematical composition of values.

misconception: Students incorrectly keep the common denominator when multiplying fractions with like denominators: (a/b)×(c/b) = (a×c)/b instead of (a×c)/(b×b). For example, (2/5)×(3/5) = 6/5 instead of the correct answer 6/25. This is an overgeneralization error where students apply the fraction addition rule (keep the common denominator) to multiplication. Newton et al. (2014) found students were particularly prone to this error on like-denominator problems.

problems.problem_text: A recipe calls for 1/3 cup of ingredient A. You need 1/3 of that amount of ingredient B, and 1/3 of that amount of ingredient C. How much of ingredient C do you need in total (in cups)?
correct_steps: Problem: A recipe calls for 1/3 cup of ingredient A. You need 1/3 of that amount of ingredient B, and 1/3 of that amount of ingredient C. How much of ingredient C do you need in total (in cups)?
CORRECT METHOD: Multiply numerators AND denominators
To multiply fractions, we multiply numerators AND denominators. Even though fractions share denominator 3, we still multiply it.
malrule_steps: Problem: A recipe calls for 1/3 cup of ingredient A. You need 1/3 of that amount of ingredient B, and 1/3 of that amount of ingredient C. How much of ingredient C do you need in total (in cups)?
MALRULE: Keep the common denominator (treating multiplication like addition)
Both fractions have denominator 3, so keep it
The student incorrectly keeps the common denominator 3, overgeneralizing the addition rule to multiplication. In multiplication, we must multiply both numerators AND denominators.

problems.problem_text: Multiply: 2 2/5 × 3 1/5
correct_steps: CORRECT METHOD: Multiply numerators AND denominators
To multiply fractions, we multiply numerators AND denominators. Even though fractions share denominator 5, we still multiply it.
malrule_steps: MALRULE: Keep the common denominator (treating multiplication like addition)
Both have denominator 5, so keep it
The student incorrectly keeps the common denominator 5, overgeneralizing the addition rule to multiplication. In multiplication, we must multiply both numerators AND denominators.

misconception: Students count ALL zeros in a number when determining the exponent for scientific notation, without considering their placement. They don't distinguish between leading zeros, trailing zeros, and zeros between significant digits. Instead of counting decimal places moved, they simply count zeros and use that as the exponent magnitude.

problems.problem_text: Express 0.0080334 in scientific notation.
correct_steps: Step 1: Find the first non-zero digit

For products less than 10, they write the result normally.

Example: 68 x 46 = 24 (correct: 3128)

misconception: Students evaluate arithmetic expressions strictly from left to right, ignoring operator precedence rules (PEMDAS/BODMAS). They fail to identify that median is more appropriate for skewed data.

This is documented in Brown & Burton's 1978 paper on diagnostic models for procedural bugs in basic mathematical skills.

misconception: A widespread misconception where students believe division always produces a result smaller than the dividend. Fischbein et al. (1985) identified this as a 'primitive intuitive model' stemming from early division experiences with whole numbers. When dividing by decimals or fractions less than 1 (which mathematically produces a larger result), students reject the correct answer as impossible and switch to multiplication. For example, students find 4 ÷ 0.5 = 8 counterintuitive and switch to 4 × 0.5 = 2 instead.

They add or subtract percentages directly without recognizing that each percentage applies to a different base value. This reflects a fundamental gap in the transition from additive to multiplicative reasoning, which is one of the major barriers to mathematical development (Van Dooren, De Bock, & Verschaffel, 2010).

misconception: A systematic procedural bug in addition where the student forgets to reset the carry register to zero after processing each column. Instead of resetting the carry after adding it to a column, the carry value accumulates across columns. For example, in 328 + 917, the student writes 5 (from 8+7=15), carries 1, then computes 2+1+1=4, but instead of resetting the carry to 0, keeps it at 1. In the next column, 3+9+1=13, so the final answer is 1345 instead of 1245. This bug was identified by Brown & Burton (1978) in their BUGGY diagnostic system for arithmetic procedures.

misconception: Students terminate the factoring process prematurely, stopping after one factoring step without recognizing that further factorization is possible. For example, writing 2x² - 8 = 2(x² - 4) instead of the complete factorization 2(x+2)(x-2). This reflects a procedural rather than conceptual understanding of what 'factor completely' means (Kieran, 1992; Vaiyavutjamai & Clements, 2006).

problems.problem_text: The volume of a geometric shape is x³ - 25x cubic units. Factor this expression completely.
correct_steps: Word Problem: The volume of a geometric shape is x³ - 25x cubic units. Factor this expression completely.
Step 1: Extract the expression from the word problem
Strategy: Factor until no more factoring is possible
Step 3: Factor out the common variable x
Step 4: Check if the factored part can be factored further
This is a difference of squares!
Step 5: Apply difference of squares formula
Final Step: Verify it's completely factored
Each factor is either a number or linear (cannot factor further)
malrule_steps: Word Problem: The volume of a geometric shape is x³ - 25x cubic units. Factor this expression completely.
Step 1: Extract the expression from the word problem
Step 2: Factor (but student stops too early)
MALRULE: Stop after first factoring step (incomplete)
Student thinks: 'I factored out x, I'm done!'
WRONG! The factor (x² - 25) can be factored further! It's a difference of squares: x² - 25 = (x + 5)(x - 5). The complete factorization is x(x + 5)(x - 5).
The fundamental error: Stopping before complete factorization!

problems.problem_text: Factor completely: 3x² + 18x + 24

Final Step: Verify it's completely factored

malrule_steps: MALRULE: Stop after first factoring step (incomplete)
Student thinks: 'I factored out the GCF, I'm done!'
WRONG! The trinomial x² + 6x + 8 can be factored further! It factors as (x + 4)(x + 2) since 4 × 2 = 8 and 4 + 2 = 6. The complete factorization is 3(x + 4)(x + 2).
The fundamental error: Stopping before complete factorization!

Check: Is this a perfect square?

malrule_steps: Word Problem: A rectangular garden bed has area 5x² + 30x + 45 square meters. Express in completely factored form.
Step 1: Extract the expression from the word problem
Step 2: Factor (but student stops too early)
MALRULE: Stop after first factoring step (incomplete)
Student thinks: 'I factored out the GCF, I'm done!'
WRONG! The trinomial x² + 6x + 9 is a perfect square! Notice: 6 = 2 × 3 and 9 = 3². So x² + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)². The complete factorization is 5(x + 3)².
The fundamental error: Stopping before complete factorization!

misconception: When adding fractions with different denominators, students incorrectly add numerators together and denominators together, treating the operation as component-wise addition. For example: 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5 (incorrect). This error reflects a fundamental misunderstanding where students treat fractions as two independent whole numbers rather than a single quantity representing a ratio. Research shows this stems from 'whole number bias' - the overgeneralization of whole-number arithmetic properties to fractions (Ni & Zhou, 2005; Behr et al., 1984).

misconception: A widespread misconception where students believe multiplication always produces a result larger than both factors. Fischbein et al. When multiplying by decimals or fractions less than 1 (e.g., 0.5 × 0.2 = 0.1), students reject the correct answer as impossible because the product is smaller than both factors. They may substitute addition or refuse to accept the mathematically correct result.

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where the student aligns numbers on the left side instead of the right side (place value alignment) when adding numbers of different digit lengths. This causes the shorter number to be effectively multiplied by a power of 10. For example, in 23 + 456, the student aligns 23 with the left side of 456, treating 23 as 230, yielding 686 instead of the correct answer 479. This is documented in Brown & Burton's 1978 paper on diagnostic models for procedural bugs in basic mathematical skills.

misconception: Students don't recognize how outliers affect the mean. Research shows students are 'not only confused about the median and the mean but also unable to use and interpret information' about when each is appropriate (Zawojewski & Shaughnessy, 2000). When asked if the mean represents a data set with outliers, they say 'yes' without understanding that outliers pull the mean away from typical values. They fail to identify that median is more appropriate for skewed data.

'Rise over run' = vertical change / horizontal change

Step 4: Calculate slope using CORRECT formula

misconception: When adding multi-digit numbers, students write the entire column sum directly in that column without regrouping, failing to understand the base-10 constraint that each place value position can only hold a single digit (0-9). For example, in 48+17, students compute 8+7=15 and write '15' in the ones column, producing concatenated results like '415' instead of the correct answer 65. This error, documented by the Colorado Department of Education, indicates a fundamental misunderstanding of place value.

misconception: A widespread misconception where students believe division always produces a result smaller than the dividend. Fischbein et al. (1985) identified this as a 'primitive intuitive model' stemming from early division experiences with whole numbers. When dividing by decimals or fractions less than 1 (which mathematically produces a larger result), students reject the correct answer as impossible and switch to multiplication. For example, students find 4 ÷ 0.5 = 8 counterintuitive and switch to 4 × 0.5 = 2 instead.

MALRULE REASONING: Division must make it smaller, not bigger

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where the student forgets to borrow over blank columns when the minuend (top number) has fewer digits than the subtrahend (bottom number). The student incorrectly processes the 'blank' positions (implicit zeros) without properly propagating borrows. For example, in 85 - 127, the student may treat the hundreds column as simply 1-0 or 0-1 (using smaller-from-larger), yielding an incorrect positive result instead of recognizing that the operation produces a negative number or requires special handling. This bug is located in the COLUMN SEQUENCE procedure of Brown & Burton's procedural network.

misconception: Student incorrectly applies the multiplicative (homogeneous) property of linear functions to nonlinear functions: f(cx) = c·f(x). This is a manifestation of the 'illusion of linearity' (De Bock et al., 2007), where students overgeneralize properties that hold only for linear functions f(x) = kx. Matz (1982) identified f(ka) = kf(a) as a common algebraic error.

malrule_steps: Problem: Volume scales as V(r) = r³. Calculate V(4×3).

The fundamental error: Confusing f(cx) with c·f(x). Input multiplication and output multiplication are NOT the same!

misconception: Students incorrectly compare fractions by focusing on the denominator value, believing that a larger denominator means a larger fraction. Students fail to understand the inverse relationship: larger denominators mean smaller pieces.

misconception: When subtracting fractions with different denominators, students incorrectly subtract the numerators AND subtract the denominators: a/b - c/d = (a-c)/(b-d). For example: 3/4 - 1/2 = (3-1)/(4-2) = 2/2 = 1 (incorrect; correct answer is 1/4). Brown & Quinn (2006) documented this error in their analysis of algebra students' fraction errors, finding that students 'demonstrated the error of adding or subtracting numerators and denominators across' by extending whole number operations to fractions.

misconception: Students terminate the factoring process prematurely, stopping after one factoring step without recognizing that further factorization is possible. For example, writing 2x² - 8 = 2(x² - 4) instead of the complete factorization 2(x+2)(x-2). This reflects a procedural rather than conceptual understanding of what 'factor completely' means (Kieran, 1992; Vaiyavutjamai & Clements, 2006).

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where the student always subtracts the smaller digit from the larger digit in each column, regardless of position (minuend or subtrahend). This is one of the most extensively documented subtraction bugs in cognitive science research, identified through the BUGGY and DEBUGGY diagnostic systems.

This represents what Graeber & Johnson (1991) classified as 'overgeneralization' - one of the four main types of mathematical misconceptions.

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where, when a column sum exceeds 9, the student adds the units digit and carry digit together and writes that combined result in the current column. The carry is NOT propagated to the next column. For example, in 17 + 5, the ones column computes 7+5=12, then the student adds 1+2=3 and writes 3 in the ones column. misconception: When adding fractions with different denominators, students incorrectly add numerators together and denominators together, treating the operation as component-wise addition. For example: 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5 (incorrect). This error reflects a fundamental misunderstanding where students treat fractions as two independent whole numbers rather than a single quantity representing a ratio. Research shows this stems from 'whole number bias' - the overgeneralization of whole-number arithmetic properties to fractions (Ni & Zhou, 2005; Behr et al., 1984).

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where the student writes the carry digit and forgets to write the units digit in the answer when a column sum is 10 or more. misconception: A widespread misconception where students believe division always produces a result smaller than the dividend. Fischbein et al. When dividing by decimals or fractions less than 1 (which mathematically produces a larger result), students reject the correct answer as impossible and switch to multiplication. malrule_steps: Problem: A recipe uses 3 eggs and 4 cups of milk. If you scale the recipe by a factor of 2, how much of each ingredient do you need?
MALRULE: 'Scale by 2' means ADD 2 to each ingredient

Step 2: Add 2 to second ingredient: 4 + 2 = 6 cups of milk
Scaled recipe: 5 eggs and 6 cups of milk (INCORRECT!)

misconception: A systematic procedural bug in addition where the student forgets to reset the carry register to zero after processing each column. Instead of resetting the carry after adding it to a column, the carry value accumulates across columns. For example, in 328 + 917, the student writes 5 (from 8+7=15), carries 1, then computes 2+1+1=4, but instead of resetting the carry to 0, keeps it at 1. In the next column, 3+9+1=13, so the final answer is 1345 instead of 1245. This bug was identified by Brown & Burton (1978) in their BUGGY diagnostic system for arithmetic procedures.

misconception: Students incorrectly apply the multiplication rule 'two negatives make a positive' to subtraction and addition operations. This represents what Makonye & Fakude (2016) term 'surface understanding' where students remember rules like 'negative and negative becomes positive' and apply them indiscriminately across operations. For example, students compute -5 - 6 = 11 because they see the negative sign in -5 and the subtraction operation as 'two negatives' that should combine to make a positive result. Vlassis (2004) identifies this as stemming from students' failure to distinguish between the 'operative sign' (subtraction) and the 'unary, predicative sign' (negativity of a number).

This is a concept image/concept definition gap identified by Vinner & Dreyfus (1989) - students accept the formal definition but rely on personal experience when classifying relations, often accepting multi-valued relations as functions.

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where the student always sums up all the digits with no regard to columns or place value. Instead of aligning digits by place value (ones with ones, tens with tens, etc.) and adding column by column with carrying, the student simply adds every individual digit together to get a single sum. For example, in 17 + 5, the student computes 1 + 7 + 5 = 13 instead of correctly aligning and adding to get 22. This is documented in Brown & Burton (1978) as one of the fundamental addition bugs that shows complete misunderstanding of place value.

Research shows this stems from students processing 'numerator and denominator as two separate whole numbers' (Pitkethly & Hunting, 1996; Nunes & Bryant, 1996).

When encountering 0 - N, the student treats this as equivalent to N - 0 = N, avoiding the need to borrow.

misconception: A widespread misconception where students believe multiplication always produces a result larger than both factors. Fischbein et al. (1985) identified this as stemming from the 'primitive intuitive model' of multiplication as repeated addition, where results are always larger with whole numbers. When multiplying by decimals or fractions less than 1 (e.g., 0.5 × 0.2 = 0.1), students reject the correct answer as impossible because the product is smaller than both factors. They may substitute addition or refuse to accept the mathematically correct result.

misconception: Students incorrectly believe that percentage relationships are symmetric or reversible. They assume that if a value increased by X%, it can return to the original by decreasing X%, or that if A is X% of B, then B is X% of A. This misconception stems from overgeneralizing the commutative property of addition and multiplication to percentage relationships, which are inherently asymmetric because each percentage is calculated relative to a different base value.

Key insight: Percentage relationships depend on the BASE value!
malrule_steps: MALRULE REASONING: 'The percentage works the same both ways'
INCORRECT! Percentage relationships are NOT symmetric.
The percentage depends on which value is the base (denominator).

misconception: Students fail to understand the univalence requirement: that functions must map each input to exactly ONE output. This is a concept image/concept definition gap identified by Vinner & Dreyfus (1989) - students accept the formal definition but rely on personal experience when classifying relations, often accepting multi-valued relations as functions.

malrule_steps:
Problem: Consider this mapping diagram:
  18 → 3
  18 → 11
  20 → 9

Does this mapping represent a function?...
MALRULE: Any set of ordered pairs is a function
MALRULE REASONING: 'If it has inputs and outputs, it's a function'
'Don't need to check for repeated inputs' [WRONG!]

Yes, every input has an arrow pointing to an output
'Since all inputs map to outputs, it's a function'

misconception: Student thinks a^0 = 0 instead of a^0 = 1. For example, 5^0 = 0 instead of 5^0 = 1. Research by Ulusoy (2019) found only 30.9% of students correctly answered that a^0 = 1.

CORRECT METHOD: Apply zero exponent rule
At chapter 0 (the start), the multiplier is 1 (original amount)
The key insight is that a^0 = 1 is NOT arbitrary! It follows from the pattern of exponents and from the division rule. Any non-zero number raised to the zero power equals 1.
malrule_steps: Problem: The number of pages in a book doubles every chapter, following the pattern 4^c for chapter c. How many times the original is it at chapter 0 (the start)?
MALRULE: Zero exponent means zero result
Reasoning: 'At the start (chapter 0), the multiplier is 0'
The student incorrectly interprets the zero exponent as producing zero. They don't understand that a^0 = 1 by definition and by the exponent division rule.

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where, when a column sum exceeds 9, the student adds the units digit and carry digit together and writes that combined result in the current column. The carry is NOT propagated to the next column. For example, in 17 + 5, the ones column computes 7+5=12, then the student adds 1+2=3 and writes 3 in the ones column. The tens column then computes 1+0=1. Result: 13 instead of 22. This bug may arise from confusion about Method 2 (left-to-right addition) where carries are written under the same column.

misconception: When adding fractions with different denominators, students incorrectly add numerators together and denominators together, treating the operation as component-wise addition. For example: 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5 (incorrect). This error reflects a fundamental misunderstanding where students treat fractions as two independent whole numbers rather than a single quantity representing a ratio. Research shows this stems from 'whole number bias' - the overgeneralization of whole-number arithmetic properties to fractions (Ni & Zhou, 2005; Behr et al., 1984).

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where the student writes the carry digit and forgets to write the units digit in the answer when a column sum is 10 or more. For example, in 87 + 93, the student computes 7+3=10, writes 1 (the carry digit) instead of 0, then 8+9=17, writes 1 (the carry digit) instead of 7, yielding 11 instead of the correct answer 180. This bug was documented by Brown & Burton (1978) in their analysis of systematic procedural errors in arithmetic.

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where the student always subtracts the smaller digit from the larger digit in each column, regardless of position (minuend or subtrahend). This error avoids borrowing by reversing the subtraction when the top digit is smaller than the bottom digit. For example, in 62 - 37, the student computes 7-2=5 in the ones column (instead of borrowing) and 6-3=3 in the tens column, yielding 35 instead of the correct answer 25. This is one of the most extensively documented subtraction bugs in cognitive science research, identified through the BUGGY and DEBUGGY diagnostic systems.

misconception:
A compound procedural bug where the student's multiplication algorithm mimics the column behavior of addition---multiplying column by column instead of digit by digit. The student processes corresponding digits in each column (like in addition), but multiplies them instead of adding. Additionally, the student applies the WRITE/CARRY/FORGET/UNITS bug: when a column product is 10 or greater, they write only the carry digit (tens place) and forget the units digit. For products less than 10, they write the result normally.

Example: 68 x 46 = 24 (correct: 3128)
  - Column 1 (ones): 8 x 6 = 48, writes 4 (the carry), forgets 8
  - Column 2 (tens): 6 x 4 = 24, writes 2 (the carry), forgets 4
  - Final answer: 24

misconception: Student multiplies exponents when multiplying powers with the same base: x^m × x^n = x^(m×n). For example, x³ × x⁵ = x¹⁵ instead of x⁸. Research documents this as confusion between the product rule (add) and power rule (multiply).

Then, divide: x^7 ÷ x^4 = x^(7-4) = x^3
Multiplying gives 7 factors, dividing by x^4 removes 4 factors
The product rule states that when multiplying powers with the same base, we add the exponents.

The student incorrectly multiplies the exponents when multiplying powers with the same base. The correct rule is to ADD the exponents.

The product rule states that when multiplying powers with the same base, we add the exponents.
malrule_steps: The student incorrectly multiplies the exponents. This confuses the product rule (add exponents) with the power rule (multiply exponents for (x^m)^n).

misconception: Students confuse decimal places with significant figures. When asked to round to N significant figures, they instead round to N decimal places. misconception: Students incorrectly apply the multiplication rule 'two negatives make a positive' to subtraction and addition operations. This represents what Makonye & Fakude (2016) term 'surface understanding' where students remember rules like 'negative and negative becomes positive' and apply them indiscriminately across operations. For example, students compute -5 - 6 = 11 because they see the negative sign in -5 and the subtraction operation as 'two negatives' that should combine to make a positive result. Vlassis (2004) identifies this as stemming from students' failure to distinguish between the 'operative sign' (subtraction) and the 'unary, predicative sign' (negativity of a number).

misconception: When adding fractions with different denominators, students incorrectly add numerators together and denominators together, treating the operation as component-wise addition. For example: 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5 (incorrect). This error reflects a fundamental misunderstanding where students treat fractions as two independent whole numbers rather than a single quantity representing a ratio. Research shows this stems from 'whole number bias' - the overgeneralization of whole-number arithmetic properties to fractions (Ni & Zhou, 2005; Behr et al., 1984).

problems.problem_text: Find the sum of 7/4 and 13/11.

misconception: When subtracting fractions with different denominators, students incorrectly subtract the numerators AND subtract the denominators: a/b - c/d = (a-c)/(b-d). For example: 3/4 - 1/2 = (3-1)/(4-2) = 2/2 = 1 (incorrect; correct answer is 1/4). Brown & Quinn (2006) documented this error in their analysis of algebra students' fraction errors, finding that students 'demonstrated the error of adding or subtracting numerators and denominators across' by extending whole number operations to fractions.

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where the student aligns numbers on the left side instead of the right side (place value alignment) when adding numbers of different digit lengths. This is documented in Brown & Burton's 1978 paper on diagnostic models for procedural bugs in basic mathematical skills.

misconception: Students incorrectly keep the common denominator when multiplying fractions with like denominators: (a/b)×(c/b) = (a×c)/b instead of (a×c)/(b×b). For example, (2/5)×(3/5) = 6/5 instead of the correct answer 6/25. This is an overgeneralization error where students apply the fraction addition rule (keep the common denominator) to multiplication. Newton et al. (2014) found students were particularly prone to this error on like-denominator problems.

Both have denominator 5, so keep it
The student incorrectly keeps the common denominator 5, overgeneralizing the addition rule to multiplication. In multiplication, we must multiply both numerators AND denominators.

misconception: A systematic procedural bug where, when a column sum exceeds 9, the student adds the units digit and carry digit together and writes that combined result in the current column. The carry is NOT propagated to the next column. For example, in 17 + 5, the ones column computes 7+5=12, then the student adds 1+2=3 and writes 3 in the ones column. The tens column then computes 1+0=1. Result: 13 instead of 22. This bug may arise from confusion about Method 2 (left-to-right addition) where carries are written under the same column.

misconception: Students incorrectly apply the multiplication rule 'two negatives make a positive' to subtraction and addition operations. This represents what Makonye & Fakude (2016) term 'surface understanding' where students remember rules like 'negative and negative becomes positive' and apply them indiscriminately across operations. For example, students compute -5 - 6 = 11 because they see the negative sign in -5 and the subtraction operation as 'two negatives' that should combine to make a positive result. Vlassis (2004) identifies this as stemming from students' failure to distinguish between the 'operative sign' (subtraction) and the 'unary, predicative sign' (negativity of a number).

misconception: Students incorrectly keep the common denominator when multiplying fractions with like denominators: (a/b)×(c/b) = (a×c)/b instead of (a×c)/(b×b). misconception: A systematic procedural bug in addition where the student forgets to reset the carry register to zero after processing each column. Instead of resetting the carry after adding it to a column, the carry value accumulates across columns. For example, in 328 + 917, the student writes 5 (from 8+7=15), carries 1, then computes 2+1+1=4, but instead of resetting the carry to 0, keeps it at 1. In the next column, 3+9+1=13, so the final answer is 1345 instead of 1245. This bug was identified by Brown & Burton (1978) in their BUGGY diagnostic system for arithmetic procedures.

misconception: Students terminate the factoring process prematurely, stopping after one factoring step without recognizing that further factorization is possible. For example, writing 2x² - 8 = 2(x² - 4) instead of the complete factorization 2(x+2)(x-2). Step 2: Factor (but student stops too early)

Student thinks: 'I factored out the GCF, I'm done!'

The fundamental error: Stopping before complete factorization!

misconception: Students incorrectly believe that percentage relationships are symmetric or reversible. They assume that if a value increased by X%, it can return to the original by decreasing X%, or that if A is X% of B, then B is X% of A. Key insight: Percentage relationships depend on the BASE value!
malrule_steps: Problem: Value decreased from 85 to 51 (40% decrease).
What is the percent increase from 51 back to 85?
MALRULE: Decrease and increase percentages are symmetric
MALRULE REASONING: 'If it decreased by 40%, it must increase by 40%'
INCORRECT! Percentage relationships are NOT symmetric.
The percentage depends on which value is the base (denominator).

This represents what Graeber & Johnson (1991) classified as 'overgeneralization' - one of the four main types of mathematical misconceptions.

misconception: When the minuend digit is 0 and the subtrahend digit is N (where N > 0), the student writes N as the result instead of borrowing. When encountering 0 - N, the student treats this as equivalent to N - 0 = N, avoiding the need to borrow.

misconception: Students incorrectly determine the sign of the result by always using the sign of the number with the larger absolute value, regardless of the operation. This represents an overgeneralization from addition of integers with different signs (where the rule works) to all integer operations. Makonye & Fakude (2016) classify this as a 'strategic error' where students apply a partially-correct strategy inappropriately. For subtraction like 3 - (-8), students incorrectly reason: '|8| > |3|, so use -8's sign' → -11 (wrong! correct answer is +11).

misconception: Student multiplies exponents when multiplying powers with the same base: x^m × x^n = x^(m×n). For example, x³ × x⁵ = x¹⁵ instead of x⁸. Research documents this as confusion between the product rule (add) and power rule (multiply).

problems.problem_text: Three data processing stages have efficiency factors of x^4, x^4, and x^3 respectively. When these factors are multiplied together, what is the combined efficiency? (Express as x^? - provide the exponent)
correct_steps: Word Problem: Three data processing stages have efficiency factors of x^4, x^4, and x^3 respectively. When these factors are multiplied together, what is the combined efficiency? (Express as x^? - provide the exponent)

When multiplying powers with the same base, ADD the exponents:
x^4 × x^4 × x^3 = x multiplied by itself (4+4+3) = 11 times
The product rule states that when multiplying powers with the same base, we add the exponents.

misconception: Students don't recognize how outliers affect the mean. Research shows students are 'not only confused about the median and the mean but also unable to use and interpret information' about when each is appropriate (Zawojewski & Shaughnessy, 2000). When asked if the mean represents a data set with outliers, they say 'yes' without understanding that outliers pull the mean away from typical values. They fail to identify that median is more appropriate for skewed data.

misconception: Students incorrectly believe that percentage relationships are symmetric or reversible. They assume that if a value increased by X%, it can return to the original by decreasing X%, or that if A is X% of B, then B is X% of A. This misconception stems from overgeneralizing the commutative property of addition and multiplication to percentage relationships, which are inherently asymmetric because each percentage is calculated relative to a different base value.

The percentage depends on which value is the base (denominator).
